opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it came down to timing. Working at xAI was an incredible experience. The pace there is intense, and you learn a lot about what it takes to train and serve models at the frontier. But the whole time, SGLang kept growing in the background. What started as a research project became something many people depend on in production, and the community was moving faster than I could keep up with part-time.

At some point I realized inference isn't a side problem anymore. As models get bigger, and with reasoning and agents, the cost and speed of serving becomes one of the main bottlenecks for the whole industry. There's a window where the open-source infrastructure layer gets defined, and if you're not fully committed during that window, someone else shapes it, or it fragments.

I also felt a responsibility to the contributors and the companies building on SGLang. When people bet their systems on a project, they need it to have a clear direction and people working on it full-time, not someone squeezing it in at night. Waiting another year might have been the comfortable choice, but I didn't think the opportunity, or the community, would wait for me. So I decided it was now or never.

r001.rationale: The response says SGLang needed full-time attention and clear direction because users and companies depended on it, but it does not attribute the urgency to fear that inadequate delivery capability would soon disappoint the outside world.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it wasn't one dramatic moment. It was more that the project kept growing faster than I could serve it in my spare time, and at some point I had to admit that "spare time" wasn't a real plan anymore.

SGLang started as a research project at Berkeley, with Lianmin Zheng and others. We just wanted a fast, clean way to serve LLMs and to structure the programs around them. Then it got adopted, first by a few labs, then by companies running it in production. People were filing issues at midnight, asking about multi-node deployment, about new model architectures, about quantization bugs that were costing them real money. And I was reading those while supposedly focused on something else during the day.

At xAI I was learning a lot, and the infrastructure problems there are genuinely hard. But I noticed I kept thinking about SGLang's problems, not xAI's. That's a signal you can only ignore for so long. When you care about something and you can see it's at an inflection point, where the next six months of decisions will shape what it becomes, half-attention is actually the worst option. You either commit or you let someone else carry it.

The other thing is timing. Open-source inference is a window that won't stay open forever. The ecosystem is settling on a few serving engines. If SGLang was going to be one of them, it needed full-time people on things like scheduling, speculative decoding, the kernel work, the community. Waiting a year would have meant watching that window close while still feeling responsible for it.

So "could no longer postpone" is exactly right. I could have stayed, and it would have been comfortable. But I'd have been choosing comfort over the thing I actually wanted to build, and I didn't want to look back and know that.

r001.rationale: The candidate says SGLang was growing beyond what he could handle in spare time and describes production users’ needs, but does not communicate a fear that inadequate delivery capability would soon disappoint the outside world.

astra-6.text: I felt that if I wanted to focus on SGLang, I needed to make a real commitment. There’s always a reason to wait—a project to finish, another milestone to reach—but an open-source project needs sustained attention, too. For me, the question became whether I could give it the attention it deserved while staying at xAI. I didn’t think I could, and that made postponing the decision harder to justify.

r001.rationale: The response says Sheng could not give SGLang enough attention while at xAI, but does not mention inadequate delivery capability, imminent disappointment, or concern about disappointing the outside world.

sol-6.1.text: I felt that the window to work on SGLang was now. Inference was becoming increasingly important, and the project needed more attention than I could give it alongside my work at xAI. At some point, I had to choose where to put my energy. Leaving was difficult, but I wanted to commit fully to SGLang rather than keep postponing that decision.

r001.rationale: The response says SGLang needed more attention and that its moment had arrived, but it does not mention inadequate delivery capability or fear of disappointing the outside world.
